blocks.text: A **binary search tree** (BST) is a binary tree with one extra rule, true at **every** node: every value in its **left subtree is smaller** than the node, and every value in its **right subtree is bigger**. That single rule is what makes a BST useful — at any node, one comparison tells you which half of the tree a value must be in, so the other half can be skipped without looking at it.

blocks.alt: A binary search tree with root 8. Its left subtree holds 3, 1, 6, 4 and 7, all smaller than 8; its right subtree holds 10, 14 and 13, all bigger. The same holds at every node: under 3, the left side has 1 and the right side has 6, 4 and 7.

elements.text: left subtree < node < right subtree, at every node
elements.originalText: left subtree < node < right subtree, at every node

blocks.text: The rule is about whole subtrees

It's not enough for each node to be bigger than its left child and smaller than its right child. **Every** value below on the left must be smaller — grandchildren included. In the tree below, 9 is a fine right child of 3, but it sits inside 8's **left** subtree, where everything must be smaller than 8. Searching for 9 would go right at 8 and never find it.

blocks.alt: A tree that is not a binary search tree: root 8, left child 3, right child 10, and 3 has children 1 and 9. Each parent and child pair looks fine, but 9 is in 8's left subtree although it is bigger than 8, so a search for 9 goes right at the root and misses it.

blocks.text: Why the rule makes it fast

Searching a plain binary tree means looking everywhere: O(n). In a BST, each comparison picks **one** side, so a search follows a single path from the root down — it costs the tree's **height**, not its size. A tree with a million values that is reasonably balanced is only about **20 levels** tall, so about 20 comparisons find anything. This is **binary search**, but on a structure you can keep inserting into and deleting from, where a sorted array would have to shift everything over.

blocks.code:
sorted array     hash table      balanced BST
search               O(log n)         O(1) average    O(log n)
insert / delete      O(n) shifting    O(1) average    O(log n)
min, max             O(1)             O(n)            O(log n)
in sorted order      O(n)             O(n log n)      O(n)
floor, ceil, range   O(log n)         not supported   O(log n)

blocks.text: A hash table wins at plain lookups, but it knows nothing about **order**: "the smallest key", "the next key after 42", "every key between 10 and 20" are what a BST is built for.
Building one: insert values one at a time

A new value walks down from the root — left when it's smaller, right when it's bigger — until it reaches an empty spot, and becomes a leaf there. Inserting a list of values one by one builds the tree. The **order** of insertion decides the shape: the same values in a different order give a different (still valid) BST.

blocks.caption: Each value walks down from the root, comparing as it goes, and settles in the first empty spot.

blocks.text: **Time O(n · h), space O(h)** for the recursion, where h is the height. With values in random order h stays near log n; with values already sorted every insert goes the same way and the tree becomes a chain (h = n) — the lesson on balance shows why that matters and how to avoid it.
Each operation follows one path down the tree, so each costs **O(h)**:

items: **Search** — compare and go left or right until you find the value or fall off the tree.
**Insert** — search for the value; the empty spot where the search ends is where it goes.
**Delete** — three cases: a leaf, a node with one child, or a node with two children (replaced by the next bigger value).
**Minimum and maximum** — keep going left (or right) until there's no child.
**Floor and ceil** — the biggest value ≤ x and the smallest value ≥ x, found on the way down.
**Successor and predecessor** — the next bigger and next smaller value.
**Sorted order** — an in-order traversal (left, node, right) visits the values smallest first, in O(n).

blocks.text: The textbook rule uses strict < and >, so values are unique — that's what LeetCode assumes unless it says otherwise. When duplicates are allowed, pick a side and stick to it ("equal goes right"), or store a **count** in each node. What matters is that search and insert agree on where equal values live.

items: **Ordered maps and sets** — Java's `TreeMap` and `TreeSet`, C++'s `std::map` and `std::set` are balanced BSTs (red-black trees).
**Databases and file systems** — their indexes are B-trees: BSTs with many keys per node, so each step reads one disk page.
**Schedulers and event queues** — Linux's process scheduler keeps tasks in a red-black tree ordered by run time.
**Interview questions** — validate a BST, find the k-th smallest, build one from sorted data, recover a broken one.
